To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

when individuals naturally respond to negative stimuli, lower levels of negative affect are associated with recruitment of prefrontal cortex, and higher levels of negative emotion are associated with greater amygdala responses.

lower levels of negative affect are associated with recruitment of prefrontal regions (including dorsolateral and ventromedial regions) that have previously been implicated in emotion regulation, whereas higher levels of negative emotion are associated with recruitment in brain regions (such as the amygdala) that have previously not been implicated in emotion-regulation.

when responding naturally to negative stimuli, lower levels of negative affect are associated with greater activation of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, dorsomedial pre-frontal cortex, and ventromedial prefrontal coex, whereas higher levels of negative effect are associated with greater amygdala activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural bases of emotion regulation, and more specifically, with the brain systems that support uninstructed emotion modulation.
the neural bases of uninformed emotion regulation, which is the most common type of emotion regulation in everyday life.
how people regulate negative affect in everyday life and how the brain supports such regulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural basis of uninstructed regulation of emotion is a combination of instructed and uninstructed regulation.
the brain regions that are active during instructed reapapraisal of negative emotion are also recruited during uninstructed emotion modulation.

the neural bases of uninformed negative emotion modulation are a combination of two processes: moment-to-moment emotion modulation depends on the dorsolateral and the dorsomedial pre-frontal cortex and individual differences in negative emotion modulation depend on the ventromedial pre-frontal Cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ventromedial prefrontal region is a key region for individual differences in the ability to regulate negative affect, and that the amygdala is a key region that is sensitive to the degree to which an individual is able to modulate negative affect.
uninstructed negative affect modulation is supported by a combination of reappraisal and fear extinction processes.
uninstructed regulation of negative affect involves both moment-to-moment and individual differences processes that are similar in nature to instructed regulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can learn a lot by studying how people naturally regulate their emotions.
the ability to regulate one's emotional response is not a fixed trait but rather is a dynamic process that is sensitive to both situational factors and individual differences.
we are not passive bystanders to our own emotions.
